Concomitance
kŏn-kŏm´ĭ-tans
n. (the doctrine that the whole Christ is present under either eucharistic species, used to justify withholding the cup from the laity)
Latin concomitari, to accompany. Defined at Constance in 1415, which conceded that Christ instituted the sacrament in both kinds and withheld the cup anyway.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Concomitance holds that because the living Christ is undivided, His blood accompanies His body under the bread, so the cup may be withheld from the people without loss. The institution is against it in the plainest words the Lord could have used: “he took the cup, and gave thanks, and gave it to them, saying, Drink ye all of it” (Mat 26:27); Mark records the obedience, “and they all drank of it” (Mar 14:23); Paul delivers the same rite to a Gentile church, “this cup is the new testament in my blood: this do ye, as oft as ye drink it, in remembrance of me” (1Co 11:25), and states the double sign twice over: “as often as ye eat this bread, and drink this cup, ye do shew the Lord's death till he come” (1Co 11:26).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines concomitance as a being together, or in connection with another thing; and concomitant as accompanying, conjoined with, concurrent.

expand to see more

CONCOMITANCE, CONCOMITANCY, n. A being together or in connection with another thing.

CONCOMITANT, a. Accompanying; conjoined with; concurrent; attending.

CONCOMITANT, n. A companion; a person or thing that accompanies another, or is collaterally connected.

Key Scripture

Mat 26:27 — "And he took the cup, and gave thanks, and gave it to them, saying, Drink ye all of it;"

Mar 14:23 — "And he took the cup, and when he had given thanks, he gave it to them: and they all drank of it."

1Co 11:25 — "After the same manner also he took the cup, when he had supped, saying, This cup is the new testament in my blood: this do ye, as oft as ye drink it, in remembrance of me."

1Co 11:26 — "For as often as ye eat this bread, and drink this cup, ye do shew the Lord's death till he come."

Modern Corruption

A clever inference is used to overturn a command, and the command was three words long.

expand to see more

The argument is not stupid. If Christ is risen and undivided, then wherever He is present He is wholly present, and the reasoning that follows from it is coherent. What the reasoning does is set aside Drink ye all of it — a direct imperative, spoken at the institution, with a word (all) that anticipates the very restriction later imposed. Mark notes that they all drank. Paul repeats the rite to a church far from that upper room and includes the cup each time he names the bread. When a theological inference, however tidy, ends by cancelling a plain command of the Lord about His own supper, the inference is what must give way.

The instinct underneath it is worth naming, because it is not confined to Rome: an anxiety about the people. The cup was withheld partly from fear of spillage, partly from a settled sense that the laity are a lesser order who may safely be given less. Every clericalism produces some version of that — a table fenced by the wrong criteria, a Bible effectively reserved to the trained, a worship in which the congregation watches. First Corinthians 11 was written to correct abuses at the table by putting the whole institution back into the hands of the whole church, which is what the apostle had received of the Lord and delivered unto them.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek poterion (G4221), cup; pino (G4095), to drink; diatheke (G1242), covenant, testament; anamnesis (G364), remembrance.

expand to see more

Greek poterion (G4221) — cup; Matthew 26:27, Mark 14:23, 1 Corinthians 10:16, 11:25–28.

Greek pinete ex autou pantes (G4095) — drink ye all of it; Matthew 26:27 — the imperative with pantes.

Greek anamnesis (G364) — remembrance; Luke 22:19, 1 Corinthians 11:24–25.

Usage

"“Drink ye all of it” — three words, and the doctrine sets them aside."

"“And they all drank of it” — Mark records the obedience."

"“As oft as ye drink it” — delivered to a Gentile church years later."
